common_name: Norseman African Violet (Historic Original Ten True-Blue Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Norseman was one of the original ten African violet cultivars released by Armacost & Royston, the California nursery that launched the species into American commerce.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow on as a houseplant in bright indirect light, never direct sun, in slightly acidic, well-drained potting mix. Norseman produces a heavy, near-continuous flush of medium true-blue single flowers over a compact rosette of dark, fuzzy foliage, and was prized among the original ten Armacost & Royston selections as the bluest of the batch, a color still used as a benchmark by breeders today. Water from below or carefully at the soil line to keep moisture off the crown and leaves, and feed lightly every three to four weeks during active growth. Divide or restart from leaf cuttings periodically, since older crowns can become leggy and lose vigor over time.

common_name: Sailor Boy African Violet (Historic Original Ten Sea-Blue Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Sailor Boy was among the original ten African violet cultivars introduced by Armacost & Royston, the nursery credited with popularizing the species in the United States.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained potting mix, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Sailor Boy is a free-flowering member of the historic original ten, bearing bright sea-blue single flowers held well above a rosette of glossy, dark green foliage, and remains sought after by collectors for its place at the origin of the African violet's commercial history. Avoid splashing water on the leaves or crown to prevent rot and unsightly spotting, and rotate the pot regularly so the symmetrical rosette does not lean toward the light. Repot every year or two into fresh mix as the lower leaves are removed and the crown gradually rises.

common_name: Rhapsodie Michele African Violet (Pink Bicolor Commercial Series Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Introduced in 1987 by Holtkamp Greenhouses, Rhapsodie Michele is part of the widely distributed Rhapsodie series bred for easy home culture.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained potting mix, watering when the top of the mix feels dry to the touch. Rhapsodie Michele carries pink, star-shaped single flowers edged in a speckled magenta-purple over compact dark green foliage, a pattern that made the Rhapsodie series, bred by Holtkamp Greenhouses for uniform, floriferous growth, a fixture of florist and supermarket African violet displays since the late 1980s. Feed at quarter strength with every watering or monthly at full strength with a fertilizer formulated for African violets, and remove faded flowers and their stems to keep the plant blooming steadily. Provide 12 to 14 hours of bright, indirect light daily for the heaviest bloom.

common_name: Harlequin Blue Streptocarpus (Chelsea Flower Show Bicolor Cape Primrose)

planting.note: Divide crowded clumps or root leaf cuttings in spring; grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix. Harlequin Blue, bred by Dibleys Nurseries, won the RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Year award in 2010 and was later named Chelsea Plant of the Decade.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light, away from direct sun, in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, letting the top of the mix dry slightly between waterings. Harlequin Blue was the first flat-flowering, bicolor Streptocarpus, its baby-blue upper petals and butter-yellow lower petals separated by deep purple throat streaks, a novel flower form that earned it the RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Year title in 2010 and the President's Award for Plant of the Decade. It flowers over an unusually long season on short, compact stems held just above the basal foliage, making it well suited to a windowsill or covered patio in summer. Divide congested clumps every year or two, remove spent flower stems at the base, and feed lightly during the growing season to sustain its extended bloom.

common_name: Albatross Streptocarpus (Classic White-Flowered AGM Cape Primrose)

planting.note: Divide crowded clumps or root leaf cuttings in spring; grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix. Albatross holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit and is one of the longest-established white-flowered Streptocarpus cultivars in cultivation.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, watering thoroughly and then allowing the top layer to dry before watering again. Albatross bears large, lax clusters of pure white flowers with a yellow-tinted throat over a rosette of long, strap-shaped leaves, a strong, reliable form long valued for cutting and for brightening shaded corners where fewer flowering houseplants will perform. Its RHS Award of Garden Merit reflects its consistent vigor and free flowering habit under typical indoor conditions. Remove spent flower stems and yellowing leaves regularly, and divide the rosette every couple of years to maintain a compact, floriferous clump.
